name: Content Creation for Athletes
objectives: Given one idea from your content pillars, plan a short video with a hook, value and ending, with a hook for the first 1 to 3 seconds and a call to action or clear finish, written before filming

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The three-part short video
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a short video with a hook, value and ending.
This lesson builds toward: Given one idea from your content pillars, you will plan a short video with a hook, value and ending, with a hook for the first 1 to 3 seconds and a call to action or clear finish, written before filming.
Short videos are often watched for only a second or two before people scroll. The first moment, called the hook, decides if they stay.
Plan three parts: 1. Hook (first 1 to 3 seconds): a question, a surprising moment, or a bold line like "The drill that fixed my jump shot." 2. Value (the middle): show the drill, the moment or the tip. 3. Ending: a call to action like "Save this for practice" or a satisfying finish.
Write the plan before you film. An AI assistant can give you ten hook ideas: "Give me 10 short hooks for a video showing my 5-minute footwork warm-up for basketball."
Step by step:
- Pick one idea from your content pillars.
- Write a hook for the first 1-3 seconds.
- List the shots that show the value.
- Write the ending or call to action.
- Ask AI for more hook ideas and pick the best.
Words to know:
- Hook: the first 1 to 3 seconds that make people want to keep watching.
- Call to action: a clear next step you ask viewers to take.
Try it now: Write a three-part plan for one short video. Ask an AI assistant for ten hooks and choose the one that fits you best.
You can now plan a short video with a hook, value and ending.

check.q: What are the three parts of a short video plan?
check.why: Plan a hook, the value in the middle, and an ending.

check.q: Your video idea is a cool-down stretch routine. What do you do before filming?
options: Write the hook, the shots and the ending
Ask a teammate to film anything
check.why: Write the plan before you film so you know what shots you need.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Filming with your phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Film clean clips with good light, steady framing and clear sound.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone, you will film clean vertical clips with good light, steady framing and clear sound, facing the light, with the action centered and permission from anyone else in the shot.
Light: face the light, not away from it. Daylight from a window or outdoors in the shade is great. Avoid filming with a bright window behind you.
Framing and steadiness: film vertically for short-video apps, keep the phone steady with a tripod or by leaning on something, and keep the action in the middle of the frame. Wipe your lens first. Slow-motion mode is great for showing technique.
Sound: if you are talking, get close to the phone and away from wind and loud gyms, or add voice-over later. Ask permission before filming teammates, coaches or other people, and follow your team's filming rules.
Step by step:
- Wipe the lens.
- Face the light.
- Film vertically and steady.
- Keep the action centered.
- Record a few extra seconds before and after each clip.
- Ask permission before filming others.
Words to know:
- Vertical video: video filmed with the phone upright, the shape most short-video apps use.
- Voice-over: talking recorded separately and added on top of the video.
Try it now: Film the clips for your planned video. Shoot each one twice and keep the best take.
You can now film clean, steady clips with good light and sound.

check.q: Which way should you hold your phone for short-video apps?
You are filming in front of a bright window and your face looks dark. What do you do?
options: Turn so you face the window light
check.why: Face the light, not away from it.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Telling a story in your clips
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Choose and order clips so the video tells a short story.
This lesson builds toward: Given your clips, you will choose and order wide, medium and close-up shots to tell a problem, work, result story, with every clip helping the story and no faked results.
Even a 30-second video can tell a story: a problem, the work, the result. "I kept missing left-handed layups. Here's the drill I did every day for two weeks. Now look."
Use different shots: a wide shot to show where you are, a medium shot for the action, and a close-up for details like footwork or hands. Switching shots keeps people watching.
Behind-the-scenes and real moments, like early workouts, team bus rides or a thank-you to a coach, often connect better than perfect highlight edits. Stay honest; do not fake results.
Step by step:
- Write your story in one line: problem, work, result.
- Pick a wide, medium and close-up clip.
- Order them to match the story.
- Cut anything that does not help the story.
Words to know:
- Wide shot: shows the whole scene and where you are.
- Close-up: a tight shot of a detail, like hands or feet.
Try it now: Write your video's story in one line, then put your clips in order: at least one wide, one medium and one close-up.
You can now order clips into a short, honest story with varied shots.

check.q: What does a wide shot show?
check.why: A wide shot shows the setting; medium shows action and close-up shows details.

check.q: One clip is fun but does not fit your problem, work, result story. What do you do?
check.why: Cut anything that does not help the story.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Editing with a free app
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Edit your clips into a tight video with text and music you are allowed to use.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free editing app, you will edit your clips into a 30-to-60-second video with on-screen text, captions and licensed music, with no dead time, text readable on a phone and captions checked for mistakes.
Free editors like CapCut, your phone's built-in photo app, or the editing tools inside Instagram, TikTok and YouTube Shorts let you trim clips, put them in order and add text.
Cut tight: trim the start and end of every clip so there is no dead time. Add short on-screen text for the hook and key points, big enough to read on a phone. Add captions (subtitles), since many people watch with the sound off, and check them for mistakes.
Music: use the app's built-in licensed music library or royalty-free tracks. Using a popular song from somewhere else can get your video muted or removed, and sponsored posts may have stricter music rules.
Step by step:
- Import your clips in order.
- Trim dead time at the start and end of each clip.
- Add hook text in the first seconds.
- Add captions and check them.
- Add music from the app's library.
- Watch it once full screen on your phone.
Words to know:
- Trim: cut off the parts of a clip you do not need.
- Captions: words on screen that show what is said.
- Royalty-free music: music you can use under its license without paying per use.
Try it now: Edit your video to 30-60 seconds with hook text, captions and music from the app's library. Watch it full screen and cut anything slow.
You can now edit a tight short video with text, captions and allowed music.

check.q: Where should you get music for your video?
options: The app's licensed music library or royalty-free tracks
check.why: Outside songs can get your video muted or removed.

check.q: The app's auto captions spelled your coach's name wrong. What do you do?
options: Remove your coach from the video
check.why: Add captions and check them for mistakes.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Captions and posts with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a post caption with AI help, in your voice, with honest disclosures.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant, you will write a post caption in your own voice with a few relevant hashtags, tagging only people who agreed, and disclosing any brand benefit in the video and near the start of the caption.
The post caption is the text under your video. Ask an AI assistant: "Write three short captions for my video showing my footwork warm-up. Friendly, under 150 characters, end with a question to get comments."
Pick one and make it sound like you. Add a few relevant hashtags, not dozens. Tag people only if they agreed.
If a brand paid you or gave you anything for the video, say it clearly in the video (spoken and on screen) and in the caption, near the start, like "Ad" or "Thanks [brand] for the free gear". The FTC says putting it only at the end, in hashtags or in the description is not enough. College athletes: check NIL reporting rules with your compliance office.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for three short caption options.
- Rewrite your pick in your voice.
- Add a few relevant hashtags.
- If a brand is involved, disclose in the video and near the start of the caption.
- Post when your audience is usually online.
Words to know:
- Hashtag: a word with # in front that groups posts on a topic.
- Disclosure: a clear statement that a brand paid you or gave you something.
Official sources:
- FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
Try it now: Write the caption for your video with AI help, edit it into your voice, and post the video.
You can now write a short, honest post caption with AI help.

check.q: How many hashtags does the lesson suggest?
check.why: Add a few relevant hashtags, not dozens.

check.q: A sports drink brand gave you free drinks for your video. Where do you disclose it?
options: Only in hashtags at the end
Nowhere, because it was not cash
Spoken and on screen in the video, and near the start of the caption
check.why: The FTC says disclosures only at the end, in hashtags or the description are not enough.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your two-week content calendar
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan two weeks of posts in a simple calendar that fits your training.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets or a notes app, you will plan two weeks of posts in a content calendar, with 3 to 4 posts a week, Date, Pillar, Idea, Format and Status columns, and busy weeks blocked out.
Posting regularly matters more than posting a lot. Three or four posts a week is plenty for most athletes in season.
Make a calendar in Google Sheets or a notes app with columns: Date, Pillar (training, game day, off the field, lessons), Idea, Format (short video, photo, story), and Status (idea, filmed, edited, posted). Batch your work: film several clips in one session.
Ask an AI assistant to fill the first draft from your pillars and schedule, then edit it. Block out busy weeks like finals or tournaments: it is fine to post less then.
Step by step:
- Make columns: Date, Pillar, Idea, Format, Status.
- Plan 3-4 posts a week for two weeks.
- Ask AI to draft ideas from your pillars.
- Edit around games, exams and travel.
- Batch filming into one session.
Words to know:
- Content calendar: a schedule of what you will post and when.
- Batching: doing many of the same task at once, like filming five clips in one session.
Try it now: Final task: post your 30-60 second video, then build a two-week content calendar with six more post ideas, drafted with AI and edited around your schedule.
You can now plan two weeks of content in a calendar that fits your training.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Three-part plan No written plan, or the hook or ending is missing. A written hook, value and ending, done before filming. Several hooks were compared and the plan lists the wide, medium and close-up shots. Filming Dark, shaky or noisy clips, or people filmed without permission. Vertical, steady, well-lit clips with the action centered and permission from others. Uses slow motion or voice-over where it helps and extra seconds at each end for editing. Editing Dead time left in, no captions, or unlicensed music. A 30-to-60-second video with trimmed clips, readable on-screen text, checked captions and licensed music. Shot changes keep pace with a clear problem, work, result story. Caption and disclosure Copied AI text, many hashtags, or a missing brand disclosure. A caption in the athlete's voice with a few relevant hashtags and any disclosure placed correctly. Ends with a question that draws comments and is posted when the audience is online. Two-week calendar Fewer than six more ideas, or columns are missing. Six more ideas over two weeks with Date, Pillar, Idea, Format and Status, fitted around training and school. Filming is batched into one session and busy weeks are blocked out. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How many posts a week does the lesson suggest for most athletes in season?
check.why: Posting regularly matters more than posting a lot.

check.q: You have a tournament next weekend. How do you plan your calendar?
options: Cancel all posts for a month
Block out that week and post less
Film during games instead of playing
check.why: It is fine to post less in busy weeks like tournaments or finals.
